question: Podľa legendy biskup Mikuláš v noci tajne hodil do domu chudobného muža mešce zlata, preto dodnes dostávame čokoládové peniažky. Na čo potrebovali tie peniaze mužove tri dcéry?
source_excerpt: a poor man with three daughters could not afford dowries, so the girls could not marry. Nicholas secretly delivered gold on separate nights

extra.why_interesting: Slovaks find chocolate coins in the boot every year and assume they are just a random sweet. They are actually an echo of a legend about a dowry. A player can reason the answer out because it involves three daughters of a poor father.
extra.verification_notes: The legend says the gold paid dowries so the poor man's three daughters could marry (https://www.stnicholascenter.org/how-to-celebrate/resources/stories-poems/stories/vintage-stories/three-purses).

explanation: Bez vena by sa dievčatá nemohli vydať, a tak im Mikuláš potajomky pomohol. Zlaté čokoládové mince v čižme sú spomienkou na tie mešce zlata.

question: Mikuláš, ktorý nám plní čižmy, mal skutočný predobraz: biskupa z prímorského mesta Myra. V ktorej dnešnej krajine toto mesto leží?
source_excerpt: Myra was an ancient Lycian city, and today its site is the town of Demre in Antalya Province, Turkey.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture Mikuláš as a white-bearded figure from a snowy northern land. The real man lived on the warm Mediterranean coast of what is now Turkey. Players have footholds to reason with: he was an early Christian bishop, and the region was Byzantine.
extra.verification_notes: Myra's site is today's Demre in Antalya Province, Turkey, and Nicholas was its 4th-century bishop (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demre).

explanation: Myra je dnešné mestečko Demre na tureckom pobreží Stredozemného mora. Náš zasnežený Mikuláš teda pochádza z miesta, kde v decembri rastú pomaranče.
